sentences: A single bold black line splits the centre of the picture from top to bottom.
On either side, snowy rocks and bare trees pile up in layers, and far below, on a narrow path, one tiny person is walking.
This is the winter half of Autumn and Winter Landscapes, a pair of hanging scrolls by Sesshū Tōyō, a Zen monk and painter of Japan's Muromachi period.
It dates from the late fifteenth or early sixteenth century and is painted in ink alone on paper.
Each scroll is small, about 48 by 30 centimetres.
Sesshū was born in 1420 in what is now Okayama Prefecture and entered a temple as a boy.
In Kyoto he studied painting under the monk Shūbun.
In the late 1460s he sailed to Ming China with a diplomatic and trade mission, returning in 1469, and the paintings he saw there transformed his style.
Now look at the line in the middle.
It rises straight up and then simply fades into the sky.
It marks the edge of a sheer cliff, but it feels less like a real place than a design built from lines and planes.
Scholars often describe the picture as half abstract, a scene that could not exist in nature.
Now find the person on the path near the bottom.
The path leads toward a few roofs in the distance.
Next to the towering cliff these buildings look tiny, and that contrast makes the winter mountain feel even harsher.
Look closely at the rocks.
Their outlines are drawn with thick, firm strokes, while the insides are filled with short, rough touches of the brush.
Wherever the paper is left bare, its white surface becomes fresh snow.
Now look up at the sky.
It is washed with pale grey ink, heavy and cold, as if more snow is about to fall.
The branches of the trees are completely bare.
Let your eyes travel slowly from the bottom to the top.
Near rocks, the path, the buildings and far mountains follow one after another, building up depth step by step.
The museum points out that this clear, carefully reasoned structure is something not seen in landscape painting before Sesshū.
The composition is said to follow a model by Xia Gui, a Chinese court painter of the Southern Song dynasty.
Yet the brushwork and the way the picture is put together are entirely Sesshū's own.
The scroll carries his signature and a seal with his name.
The pair was long kept at Manshu-in, a temple in Kyoto, and entered the Tokyo National Museum in 1936.
It was designated a National Treasure in 1953.
Six of Sesshū's works hold that title, more than for any other single artist.
Step back and see it whole.
On a sheet of paper less than fifty centimetres tall, an entire winter mountain stands upright.
Today, try to find the single strongest line in the view in front of you.
